title: Why does your voice sound different in a recording?
sources: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America

lines.text: Why does hearing your own voice played back in a recording feel so completely cringe and unfamiliar?
lines.caps: Why does your voice sound *weird | in *recordings?

lines.text: When you listen to yourself speak, you are actually hearing two completely different sound paths.
lines.caps: You hear two *different | sound paths at *once

lines.text: You hear airborne sound waves entering your outer ears, just like everyone else does.
lines.caps: Air waves travel into your *ears | from the *outside

lines.text: Simultaneously, your vocal cord vibrations travel upward through your own facial bones and skull.
Bone conduction deepens lower frequencies, making your voice sound richer and deeper in your own head.
lines.caps: Bone conduction adds *deep | bass tones inside your *head

lines.text: An audio recording captures only the airborne sound waves, revealing how your voice actually sounds to the world.
lines.caps: A microphone hears only the *air | revealing your *true voice!

lines.text: Don't worry; everyone hates their recorded voice, but to others, it sounds completely normal.
lines.caps: Everyone hates their *voice | but you sound *great!
